t4-range-thinking: A range is the set of all hand combos a player can hold at a given decision point. "What cards does he have?" is the wrong question — you can never know a single hand for sure. "What is his range, and how much weight does each part carry?" is the answerable question. Range thinking is the key step that turns an incomplete-information game into a computable problem.

Three levels of hand reading: Level 1 only looks at your own cards; Level 2 guesses the opponent's "one hand"; Level 3 builds a range for the opponent and updates it with every action. All serious strategy discussion happens at Level 3.
The Narrative of a Range: Actions Are Filters

Every action filters the opponent's range: a UTG open narrows it to roughly the top 15%; a flop C-Bet keeps the betting range and removes the folding range; a turn check removes most strong value... By the river, a logically consistent player's range has been compressed to something very specific. Reading isn't telepathy — it's set operations along the action sequence.

Example: A tight-aggressive player opens UTG, the BTN calls. Flop K♠7♦2♣, UTG C-Bets, BTN calls. Turn 3♥, UTG fires again, BTN calls again. River 2♦, UTG shoves — his range narrative is "claiming K+ strength on all three streets": AK, KK, AA, and 77 dominate, with an occasional AQ bluff. Your KQ becomes a bluff catcher, and the decision shifts from "I have a pretty big pair of K" to "does his shoving range hold enough bluffs for the win rate my call requires" (the sizing sets the bar: a pot-size shove needs 33%, only a half-pot shove needs 25%).

Example 2 (preflop range construction): You open ~40% on the BTN and BB 3-bets to 3x. His action filters his range into {QQ+, AK, some AQo, a few A5s-A4s balancing 3-bets} — of your 40% opening range, only the top 8-10% has the right to continue (4Bet or call) right now. Range thinking starts preflop: opening width directly determines your fold-to-3-bet rate, and that fold rate is precisely where the opponent's 3-bet profit comes from.

Example 3 (street-by-street range updating): Flop Q♠8♦3♣, you bet and the opponent calls; his range is mainly {Qx, 88, 33, small/medium pairs, two-overcard draws}. The turn 2♥ is a blank — his range narrative barely changes, so you can keep firing to represent Q+. But if the turn were 9♠ (completing draws like 89s/97s in his calling range), the combos that "suddenly got strong" multiply and your double-barrel frequency should drop — range updating is a set operation done street by street, not a one-shot guess.
Range vs Range, Not Hand vs Hand

Every one of your own actions also declares a range to the opponent. High-level play is "my range vs his range": evaluating a bet isn't asking "is betting this hand good" but "how does my whole range build its bet/check mix at this node, and which part does this hand belong to?" This is the mindset prerequisite for GTO strategy (T5).

Quantitative tool for range vs range: your overall equity = Σ(share of each combo × that combo's equity vs the opponent's range)
Example: your range = {AA 6 combos, KK 6 combos}, opponent's range = {AK 16 combos}
AA vs AK is about 91%, KK vs AK about 69% → overall equity = 0.5×91% + 0.5×69% ≈ 80%
This weighted calculation replaces "my hand" and answers whether the whole range should commit at this node (concept from: MSSA Ch.1-4 range-construction methodology)

Range consistency: if your action sequence can't tell a self-consistent range story (e.g. check the flop and turn, then suddenly overbet-shove the river for nuts), observant opponents will snap-call your bluffs.

Practice with "range snapshots" in review: at the end of every street, write down three tiers of the opponent's range (value / medium / bluffs) with rough weights, then verify after showdown which street your snapshot drifted on.
t4-combinatorics: The quantitative tool of range analysis is the combinatorics you learned in T1: a pair has 6 combos, a suited hand 4, an offsuit hand 12, and any two unpaired ranks 16. When the opponent shoves the river and you must judge the "value:bluff" ratio, counting combos on both sides one by one is the only rigorous method.

Pocket pair = C(4,2) = 6 combos; when one card of that rank is on board = C(3,2) = 3 combos
Suited hand (e.g. AKs) = 4; offsuit (AKo) = 12; total (AK) = 4×4 = 16
Bluff ratio = bluff combos ÷ (value combos + bluff combos), compare with the required equity for the answer

Example: Board K♠9♦4♣2♥7♠, the opponent shoves the river and you read his value range as {KK, 99, 44, K9s} and bluffs as {A♠Q♠, A♠J♠ class missed backdoors}. Value combos = KK 3 (one K on board) + 99 3 + 44 3 + K9s 2 = 11; bluffs about 6 ⇒ bluff ratio 6/17 ≈ 35%. Required equity when calling a pot-sized bet = pot ÷ (pot + his bet + your call) = P ÷ (P+P+P) = 33% (25% is the number for a half-pot bet, not a pot-sized one). 35% sits only 2 points above 33% ⇒ at best this is a marginally +EV call: on the river there is no further betting left to win, so implied odds are zero and cannot cover the gap — the only genuine reasons to call come from blockers (does your hand remove his value combos, or leave his bluff combos alive?) and from range-reading error. The conclusion still comes entirely from counting rather than feel; counting just returns a thin profit here, not a fat one.
Every card on the board trims related combos: with one K on board, KK drops from 6 to C(3,2)=3 and AK from 16 to 12. You must count combos "looking at the board".

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces the count of specific opponent combos. When you hold A♠, the opponent's nut-flush combos like A♠X♠ drop to zero — you "block" it. Blockers turn your hole cards from mere hand strength into information about the opponent's range.

Two classic blocker applications: (1) bluff selection — bluff when holding a nut-flush blocker (e.g. a lone A♠ on a three-spade board), because the opponent's strongest calling hands are blocked and your fold equity rises; (2) bluff-catching / over-folding — when your hand blocks the opponent's bluff combos, his range skews more toward value and you should lean fold (only call when you unblock bluffs).

Example: A three-heart board and you hold A♥ (but no flush). Against a big shove, you happen to block every A♥X♥ nut-flush combo — half of the "claimed" strongest hands are falsified, boosting the credibility and success rate of both your raise-bluff and hero call.

Example 2 (preflop 4Bet spot): You hold A♠K♣ and read the opponent's 4Bet range as {AA, KK, QQ, AK}. Without a blocker the total is 6+6+6+16 = 34; holding AK: AA drops to C(3,2)=3, KK to 3, QQ stays 6, AK drops to 3×3=9 → 21 total. Do not read the rising share as good news: AKo leads none of those overpairs (AKo vs QQ ≈ 43%, dominated; the same against AA and KK), and the combos you removed are precisely AA and KK — his two strongest branches — so the QQ that dominates you climbs from 6/34 ≈ 18% to 6/21 ≈ 29%, and what is left actually raises the strength of his remaining range. Blockers turn "ahead/behind weight" into precisely computable inputs (here the computation delivers bad news), and that is what gives preflop all-in EV a foundation.
The blocker effect is marginal: it adjusts combo ratios, not rewrites the whole range. Before letting a blocker talk you into a wild play, confirm the base range analysis supports the direction.

Off-the-table drill: set up a random board, assign the opponent a range, and time yourself counting value and bluff combos. Once fluent, you only need to count the key branches in play — you can get the ratio in under 10 seconds.
t4-range-advantage: Range advantage: on a given board, one side's overall average equity is higher. Nuts advantage: one side's range contains more of the strongest combos (sets, big two pairs, nut flushes, etc.). They often point the same way but not always — distinguishing them is the key to modern postflop strategy.

Example 1: A♠K♦7♣ board, UTG opener vs BB caller. UTG's range is full of AK/AQ/AA/KK, while most of BB's strong Ax already 3-bet out of range — UTG holds both range and nut advantage and can C-Bet small and frequently with his entire range.

Example 2: 6♥5♥4♠ board, again UTG vs BB. UTG's big pairs still have overall equity (range advantage shrinks but persists), but combos like 87s, 53s, and 22 (straights/sets) live almost exclusively in BB's defense range — BB has the nut advantage. UTG's C-Bet frequency must drop sharply, while BB earns the license to check-raise and lead.

Example 3 (3-bet pot and turn flip): In a 3-bet pot you're IP on J♠T♠4♦. BB's defense range holds plenty of Jx/Tx, straight draws, and flush draws, but your range (the 3-better) has overpairs, AJ/KJ/QJ, and nut draws — double advantage on your side, so bet frequently. The turn 9♣ completes KQ straights — KQ is far more common in your range than BB's (his defense range barely contains pure KQ), and the nut advantage tilts further toward you; you can even overbet directly.

Quick judgment: high boards (A/K high) favor the preflop raiser; low connected boards (small/medium connectors) favor the preflop caller (especially BB, whose defense range keeps all the small cards). The wetter the board, the more important nut-advantage ownership becomes.

Quantitative framework (compute per flop):
Range advantage = your overall range equity vs the opponent's (you have it when your range-vs-range equity > 50%)
Nuts advantage = the density of your "top 5% strongest" combos ÷ the opponent's same density (> 1 means you own more nuts)
Evaluate both dimensions independently, then synthesize: double advantage → bet small and often; nut advantage alone → overbet license; neither → check frequently (concept from: Applications of NLHE Range Construction board-ownership analysis)

Range advantage sets betting frequency: the bigger your advantage, the more often you can bet (even small bets with your whole range). Nuts advantage sets the sizing ceiling: only the side with more nuts earns the right to apply oversized (overbet) pressure, because the opponent's strongest hands can only respond passively. With neither advantage, the standard play is to check frequently and control the pot.

The same framework explains turn/river "board changes": when the turn completes draws in the caller's range (e.g. a low connected board makes a fourth connected card), nut advantage changes hands and the aggressor should contract; when the turn is a blank, the existing advantage persists and you can keep firing.

Common mistake: treating "I have top pair" as a reason to bet. The correct order is to first decide whose range the board belongs to, then decide what role your specific hand plays under that strategy.
Before every flop, spend two seconds asking: "whose range does this board hit, and who holds more nut combos?" The answers basically determine this hand's frequency and sizing framework.
t4-preflop-structure: Preflop Is the First Shaping of Range Structure, Not a Verdict on One Hand

The starting-hand standards in T3 answer “can this hand open the pot”. The genuinely professional question comes later: which range does this hand live in, what is the value-to-bluff ratio inside that range, and what shape has your action filtered the opponent’s range into. Every 3-bet and 4-bet does not merely announce “I am strong” — it publishes “my range looks like this”, and the opponent can act on that. This is why a 3-bet range must carry both a value branch and a bluff branch: a value-only range is readable, and a readable range is exploitable.

Build a range in a fixed order: define the value branch first, then attach a bluff branch, and finally ask “what happens if I get moved all-in”. A range that skips the third step is transparent to your opponent: they only need to fold everything but the nuts against your raise, and your bluff branch goes bankrupt on its own.
The Mathematics of the 3-bet: α and MDF Land Preflop

Convention (identical to T5): P = pot before the action, b = what the bettor puts in this street; α = b ÷ (P + b) (the fold frequency a bluff needs to break even), MDF = P ÷ (P + b) (the minimum frequency the defender must continue).

Spot: CO opens 2.5 (blinds 0.5 + 1), BTN 3-bets to 8.
P = 0.5 + 1 + 2.5 = 4, b = 8
α = 8 ÷ (4 + 8) = 66.7% → BTN needs CO to fold about two thirds of the time for any two cards to bluff profitably
MDF(CO) = 4 ÷ 12 = 33.3% → CO must continue at least a third of their opening range
CO calling risks 5.5 (8 − 2.5) into a pot of 17.5 after the call → required equity = 5.5 ÷ 17.5 = 31.4%

The three numbers cross-check each other: the 33.3% CO continues with must actually survive the 31.4% equity threshold, otherwise MDF is compliance in name and donated money in substance. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.4 preflop range construction; The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5 the bet-fold subgame)

Example 1 (CO holds A♠Q♦, BTN 3-bets to 8, 100bb effective): calling needs 31.4% equity. AQo has about 30% against BTN’s value branch {QQ+, AK} (roughly 34 combos) and is ahead of his bluff branch — the problem is that when value dominates BTN’s 3-bets, your 30% is equity against the nuts with no positional compensation postflop. So the three-way verdict becomes explicit: calling is conditioned on the opponent’s 3-bet range being wide enough to carry bluffs; otherwise AQo belongs in the “fold” bucket, not the “call” bucket. Defaulting it to “call” replaces a range-structure judgement with an attachment to one hand.
Position Sets Sizing: OOP Must 3-bet Bigger

Same table, move the aggressor out of position: BTN opens 2.5, and after SB folds the pot is 3.5.
BB needs only 1.5 more to call → required equity = 1.5 ÷ 5 = 30% → this is why BB’s defending range can stretch to thirty-forty percent.
BB 3-bets to 11 (already has 1, increment b = 10): α = 10 ÷ (3.5 + 10) = 74.1%
Compare BTN’s IP 3-bet to 8, which needs only 66.7% folds.

The gap is not style, it is structure: the out-of-position player acts last on every street, so their equity realization is lower (detailed in T6) and they must buy more immediate fold pressure and a bigger pot to stop the same value hand from running behind. (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold’em 3-bet pots)

Example 2 (BB holds 7♠6♠: how opening size squeezes the defending range): BTN opens 2.5, SB folds, the pot is 3.5 and BB needs 1.5 to see a flop → required equity 1.5 ÷ 5 = 30%, while 7♠6♠ holds about forty percent against BTN’s wide opening range, so the call is effortless. Switch the open to 5: the pot becomes 6, BB must add 4, and the pot after the call is 10 → required equity 4 ÷ 10 = 40%. The hand’s equity is unchanged, the threshold has climbed from 30% to 40%, and a 5bb opening range is narrower and stronger, which knocks a further notch off this hand’s real equity. Threshold up, equity down: suited connectors such as 7♠6♠ are among the first hands kicked out of the defence. That is the concrete meaning of “sizing is a range tool” — opening bigger not only charges more for value, it actively surrenders the right to defend weak hands.
4-bet: Polarisation Forced by the SPR Collapse

After BTN 3-bets to 8, CO 4-bets to 20 (already has 2.5, increment b = 17.5); the pot before the action is P = 4 + 8 = 12.
α(4-bet) = 17.5 ÷ (12 + 17.5) = 59.3%
BTN must call 20 − 8 = 12 into a pot of 12 + 17.5 + 12 = 41.5 → required equity = 12 ÷ 41.5 = 28.9%
With 100bb effective stacks, both players have 80bb behind after the call → SPR = 80 ÷ 41.5 ≈ 1.9

SPR ≈ 2 means there is no room left to play postflop: three streets of betting plans collapse into “mostly all-in by the flop”. A 4-bet pot is therefore a jam-or-fold structure, not a pot you can take slowly. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.4; Applications of No-Limit Hold’em 4-bet pots)

Example 3 (the equity flip for K♣K♦ in a 4-bet pot): after CO 4-bets to 20, BTN jams to 100. CO must add 80 more, and the pot after the call is 100 + 100 + 1.5 in blinds = 201.5 → required equity = 80 ÷ 201.5 = 39.7% (about 40%). Once KK removes its own combos from the equation it holds roughly 47% against {QQ+, AK} — that clears the threshold, so calling is right. The same threshold shuts out AQo (about 30%) and JJ (about 37%): they cannot call a jam and were never worth 4-betting, so they drop back to the 3-bet or flat tiers. And if the 4-bet value branch consisted only of hands that survive a jam, it would still have to be paired with a bluff branch, or the opponent strips you cleanly with “jam anything you 4-bet, fold everything else”.

The most common way to think wrong: “I 3-bet for value.” That treats preflop as a one-street decision. The actual mechanism is that a 3-bet’s α runs as high as 66%-74%; if the opponent does not fold, your value branch has to cash out through postflop equity realization — and OOP realization is lower (T6), so a value-only 3-bet range bleeds systematically the moment the opponent defends wider. Conversely, with enough bluffs in the range the opponent is forced to widen their defence, and only then do your genuine value hands collect what they are owed.

Three-step check for building any preflop range: ① write down the combo count of the value branch (e.g. {QQ+, AK} = 6+6+6+16 = 34 combos); ② attach the bluff branch, preferring “low equity + high blocking + high realization potential” hands such as A5s (only 4 combos, and the suited ace also blocks the opponent’s nut flushes), not offhand picks like KTo that block nothing and are easily dominated; ③ ask “what do I do if I am moved all-in” — any hand that cannot answer the third question does not belong in this range.

3-bet and 4-bet sizings are not style but the solution of α and MDF: compute the required fold frequency first, then decide which range widths can carry it
Position changes realization rate, and realization rate changes sizing: OOP needs a bigger 3-bet to buy the same immediate fold pressure
With SPR near 2 the 4-bet pot is structurally jam-or-fold, so the range must be polarised and the marginal hands (AQo / JJ) stay one tier lower
Bluffs exist not only to profit on their own, but to stop the opponent from defending only against your value branch for free
t4-structure-economics: Structure Is an Independent Variable, Not Background

Every frequency and threshold in the earlier levels rests on two table parameters: how much money is already in the pot, and how much of each pot is taken away. Most players treat antes, straddles and rake as scenery - never checked when sitting down, never recomputed when changing tables. From a professional viewpoint they are independent variables in an equation: change P (the pot before an opponent acts) and α, MDF and every call threshold move with it; change μ (net winrate per 100 hands) and all the conclusions about how many hands prove an edge and how many buy-ins are safe get rewritten. This chapter fixes where each of the three parameters lands: antes and straddles move P, rake moves μ.

Do not mix the two classes of parameter. Dead-money parameters (antes, straddles, blinds already posted) change the pot P, so all frequencies and thresholds shift at once. Rake-type parameters change your net expectation μ, so everything about sample size and risk of ruin is rewritten. Mis-classify them and you reach for the wrong formula - explaining "why stealing stopped working" with a change in μ, or "why I win less" with a change in P, is the same mistake twice.
Dead Money: How Antes and Straddles Rewrite α and MDF

Same convention as the preflop structure chapter of this level: P = the pot before the opponent acts (dead money included), b = the bet size as placed, not the amount still needed to match.
Break-even fold frequency for a bluff: α = b ÷ (P + b)
Defense obligation: MDF = P ÷ (P + b)
Equity needed to call = amount still to put in ÷ pot after calling.
When P rises the direction is fixed: α falls (bluffs break even more easily), MDF rises (defense gets heavier), equity needed to call falls (the price improves). They move together by construction - all three describe the same pot. (Conceptual framing: Modern Poker Theory on ante formats)

Example 1 (an ante improves both the steal and the defense): 50/100, no ante, pot 1.5bb, BTN opens 2.25bb. α = 2.25 ÷ 3.75 = 60.0%, MDF = 40.0%; the big blind still has to put in 1.25bb to see a flop in a pot of 5.0bb, so 25.0% equity is needed. Switch to a 1bb big-blind ante (only the big blind posts it): the pot is 2.5bb, BTN still opens 2.25bb (sizing held constant to isolate the ante effect). α = 2.25 ÷ 4.75 = 47.4%, MDF = 52.6%; and because the big blind already has 1bb of blind plus 1bb of ante invested, only 0.25bb is still needed into that same 5.0bb pot, so required equity falls to 5.0%. Read the two layers together: the break-even bar for stealing drops, but getting fought back now costs more in practice - with a 5.0% threshold the big blind can defend extremely wide, so opening ranges must not loosen just because α went down. Check whether the back of your range survives a much wider defense.

Example 2 (quantifying the position gap with the same cards): after a 2.25bb open the pot is 3.75bb with no ante; the big blind 3-bets to 8bb, giving α = 8 ÷ 11.75 = 68.1% and an MDF of 31.9% for BTN. Add the 1bb big-blind ante and the pot is 4.75bb; the same 3-bet to 8bb yields α = 8 ÷ 12.75 = 62.7% and MDF = 37.3%. Out of position the bluff 3-bet now needs 5.4 fewer points of fold equity to break even, while the opener has to defend 5.4 points higher. That 68.1% + 31.9% = 100% and 62.7% + 37.3% = 100% is no coincidence: α and MDF are the two sides of a single break-even line, and moving one necessarily moves the other.
Rake: The Only Parameter That Eats μ Directly

Net winrate = gross winrate − the amount taken per 100 hands. It feeds straight into two results already derived in T1 and T8:
hands needed for significance n = (z·σ ÷ μ)², with μ in the denominator and squared, so n ∝ 1/μ²
risk of ruin under the diffusion approximation ROR = exp(−2μB ÷ σ²), shrunk by μ and by bankroll B, inflated by σ²
Convert to per-hand units before using them: μ(hand) = μ(100 hands) ÷ 100 and σ(hand) = σ(100 hands) ÷ 10. Ignoring the mild variance compression rake also brings is a deliberate simplification - the 1/μ² blow-up dwarfs that relief.

Example 3 (same skill, two different tables): you genuinely play 8bb/100, but at a micro stakes table taking about 5bb/100 you keep only 3bb/100 (rake shown as an indicative magnitude). How many hands prove the edge? With z = 1.96 and σ = 90bb/100: at 8bb/100 it takes (1.96×9 ÷ 0.08)² ≈ 48,600 hands, at 3bb/100 it takes (1.96×9 ÷ 0.03)² ≈ 345,700 hands - the ratio is exactly (8/3)² ≈ 7.1 times, which at 2000 hands a week turns half a year into three and a half. Risk of ruin on the same parameters is sharper still: σ = 9bb per hand (σ² = 81bb²) and a bankroll of B = 2000bb give exp(−2×0.08×2000 ÷ 81) = exp(−3.95) ≈ 1.9% versus exp(−1.48) ≈ 22.7%, a full order of magnitude. So the real cost of rake is not five fewer big blinds per hundred; it turns a negligible downswing into a likely one and pushes down the stakes you should be playing. (Conceptual framing: Applications of NLHE on game selection and rake impact)

Once μ is compressed, the first actions to stop paying are the ones whose single-iteration edge is tiny and which rely on mass repetition: thin 3-bet bluffs, marginal calls, small continuation aggression, and every premium you pay to keep a range balanced. What survives are thick value lines and high fold equity lines. A heavy-rake game therefore rewards a tighter, more value-forward strategy that leans on hand strength rather than on fine frequency balance. One corollary is routinely ignored: table selection is itself a source of revenue - the same skill on a softer or cheaper table is often worth more than learning another 4-bet chart.

Three questions before you sit down: 1) Does this table have an ante, and of which form (each player, big blind only, button extra)? What does P become? 2) What are the rake level and the cap, and is there any return scheme? After converting to bb/100, how much net μ do I keep? 3) Is straddle common here? Answer all three before choosing opening and defense ranges - a new table is a new equation. (Concrete rake and return percentages vary by site and stakes; this chapter gives the framework, not a lookup table.)

The classic mistake: "An ante or a straddle is just one more big blind, so the strategy does not change." The error is reading the ante as a cost instead of as a pot parameter. α = b ÷ (P + b) and MDF = P ÷ (P + b) both take P as an independent variable: a big-blind ante lifts P from 1.5bb to 2.5bb, which drops the break-even fold frequency for a steal from 60.0% to 47.4%, raises the big blind defense obligation from 40.0% to 52.6%, and cuts the price of defending from 1.25bb to 0.25bb. That is a change in frequencies, not a small overpayment - keep stealing at the old sizing and it stops working, keep defending at the old price and you hand pots away.

Hence the recomputation discipline: whenever a structural parameter changes, re-run three things - the α for steals and bluffs, MDF at each position, and the equity needed to call (count the ante inside P, and subtract what you have already posted from the amount still to put in). Before trusting any preflop chart, ask one question: under which structure was this table computed? A range chart without a structure label is a map of somebody else’s table.

Structure is an independent variable in the equation: antes and straddles lift P, which makes bluffing cheaper, defense obligations heavier and calling prices better; rake cuts μ, which makes the cost of proving the same edge rise as 1/μ² and risk of ruin expand as exp(−2μB ÷ σ²). Read the structure before you play; recompute when it changes.

t4-range-thinking-q1.question: The core claim of range thinking is:
options: Guess the exact hand the opponent holds
Treat the opponent as a set of hand combos that keeps updating with each action
Only care about your own hand strength
Memorize every hand the opponent shows down
t4-range-thinking-q1.explanation: A single hand is unknowable, but a range can be continuously inferred and updated through position and action sequences — this is the computable method of hand reading.

t4-range-thinking-q2.question: "Actions are filters" means:
options: Every action narrows the opponent's range
Actions can disguise hand strength
Only raises carry useful information
Checks convey no information
t4-range-thinking-q2.explanation: At every decision point the opponent continues with part of his range and folds the rest. Doing set operations along the action sequence narrows the range further. Checks filter too (removing most strong value).

t4-range-thinking-q3.question: After three streets of strong betting, your top pair with a weak kicker faces an all-in on the river. The correct decision framework is:
options: Top pair must call
Evaluate whether the bluff share of his shoving range meets the required equity
Decide by feel
Call because you've invested too much
t4-range-thinking-q3.explanation: Your hand is now a bluff catcher: it only beats bluffs and loses to all value. Decision = bluff share of his range vs the equity required by pot odds.

t4-range-thinking-q4.question: Under the "range vs range" view, the right question when evaluating a bet is:
options: Can my hand win if I bet?
How does my range allocate actions at this node, and which part does this hand belong to?
Will the opponent get mad?
How big should I bet to make him fold?
t4-range-thinking-q4.explanation: A single hand's action only has meaning inside the whole range's allocation — the mindset prerequisite for moving from exploitation to equilibrium thinking.

t4-range-thinking-q5.question: After the opponent 3-bets you preflop, the most accurate statement about "how his range changed" is:
options: His range is completely unknowable
The action filters the range down to strong hands plus balancing bluffs, and your continuing range narrows accordingly
A 3-bet means he must have AA
His range actually widens after a 3-bet
t4-range-thinking-q5.explanation: A 3-bet is a strong filter: the range narrows to a polarized strong-hand set, and your opening range must contract to the part entitled to continue — "actions are filters" applied preflop.

t4-combinatorics-q1.question: With one K on board, how many combos of KK can the opponent hold?
t4-combinatorics-q1.explanation: Three Ks remain: C(3,2) = 3. Every related card on the board trims combo counts — you must count while looking at the board.

t4-combinatorics-q2.question: The mechanism of a blocker is:
options: It improves your hand strength
A card you hold reduces the count of specific opponent combos
It prevents the opponent from raising
It hides your range from the opponent
t4-combinatorics-q2.explanation: Each card you hold removes every opponent combo containing that card — your hole cards thus become information about his range.

t4-combinatorics-q3.question: A three-spade board, you hold a lone A♠ (no flush). What does this mean for bluffing?
options: Nothing — you don't have a flush
You block the opponent's nut-flush combos, raising bluff success
You should fold
The opponent definitely has no flush
t4-combinatorics-q3.explanation: Holding A♠ zeroes out his A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest call/raise-back hands and boosting your bluff's fold equity. Note it trims ratios, not "definitely no flush".

t4-combinatorics-q4.question: The opponent's shoving range is 11 value combos and 6 bluff combos, facing a full-pot all-in (needs 33%). Your bluff catcher should:
options: Fold — more value combos
Call — 35% bluffs exceeds the 33% required
Raise
Depends on luck
t4-combinatorics-q4.explanation: Bluff ratio = 6/17 ≈ 35%, and calling a pot-sized bet needs P ÷ (P+P+P) = 33%, so 35% > 33% means the call profits long-term (but by only 2 points — a marginal, thin-profit call, the same arithmetic as the chapter example). "Fold — more value combos" compares raw combo counts instead of the bluff share; raising a bluff catcher turns you into the payer for his value range; "depends on luck" throws away the countable basis.

t4-combinatorics-q5.question: You hold A♠K♣ and read the opponent's 4Bet range as {AA, KK, QQ, AK}. Once the blockers count, what share of that range is QQ — the part that dominates you?
options: About 18%
About 29%
About 50%
Impossible to compute
t4-combinatorics-q5.explanation: Your AK removes 3 AA combos, 3 KK combos and 7 AK combos, shrinking the range from 34 to 21 combos while QQ stays at 6 ⇒ 6/21 ≈ 29% (about 18% is the unblocked 6/34 — the direction people misread). Do not read this as good news: AKo is behind AA, KK and QQ alike (about 43% versus QQ, i.e. dominated) and chops with AK, so the share where you are truly ahead is 0 combos — the blocker chips away exactly his strongest branches, leaving a remainder that crushes you proportionally more. This ratio is perfectly enumerable and is a key input to preflop all-in EV.

t4-range-advantage-q1.question: The difference between range advantage and nut advantage is:
options: Two names for the same concept
The former means higher overall average equity; the latter means more of the strongest combos
The former only looks preflop, the latter only at the river
The former belongs to the raiser, the latter to the caller
t4-range-advantage-q1.explanation: Range advantage is an average concept (overall equity); nut advantage is a distribution-top concept (density of strongest combos). They can diverge and carry different strategic meanings.

t4-range-advantage-q2.question: On a dry A♠K♦7♣ high board, the typical UTG-opener strategy vs BB is:
options: Only bet made hands
Frequently small C-Bet the whole range
Check everything to control the pot
Only use large bets
t4-range-advantage-q2.explanation: UTG holds both range and nut advantage on this board and BB has almost no counter combos — betting small across the full range is standard.

t4-range-advantage-q3.question: On a low connected 6♥5♥4♠ board, the nut advantage usually belongs to:
options: The UTG opener
The BB defender (who keeps small connectors and small pairs)
Whoever has position
The deeper-stacked side
t4-range-advantage-q3.explanation: Hands like 87s, 53s, and 22-66 that hit this board live almost only in BB's defense range; UTG's strong range (big cards and pairs) mostly misses.

t4-range-advantage-q4.question: What condition grants a player the license to use overbet sizes?
options: Chip lead
Holding the nut advantage
Positional advantage
Just won a big pot
t4-range-advantage-q4.explanation: Oversized sizing needs "I have more nuts than you" as support: the opponent's best hands are merely targets of my range and he can't effectively fight back.

t4-range-advantage-q5.question: Low connected 8♥7♥5♠ flop, BTN opener vs BB. The most accurate judgment is:
options: BTN has absolute range advantage and should bet the whole range
BB holds more nut combos; BTN should lower betting frequency and BB earns check-raise space
Dry board — whoever bets wins
Unrelated to preflop ranges
t4-range-advantage-q5.explanation: On low connected boards the nuts (straights, sets, two pairs) concentrate in BB's defense range, while BTN has many big cards that rarely hit — the classic "caller owns the nuts, raiser contracts" structure, and why the overbet license goes to the nut-advantage side.

t4-preflop-structure-q1.question: CO opens 2.5 and BTN 3-bets to 8. Roughly how often must BTN’s 3-bet make CO fold for it to break even as a bluff?
options: about 33%
about 50%
about 67%
about 75%
t4-preflop-structure-q1.explanation: α = b ÷ (P + b) = 8 ÷ (4 + 8) = 66.7% (here a 2x-pot 3-bet). 33% is CO’s MDF — the frequency they must continue, complementary to α and the easiest pair of numbers to swap; 50% is the α of a pot-sized bet (b = P); 75% needs roughly a 3x-pot sizing, because the fold requirement rises monotonically with bet size and never falls.

t4-preflop-structure-q2.question: Continuing: if CO calls (risking 5.5 into a pot of 17.5 after the call), what is the minimum equity required?
options: about 23%
about 31%
about 40%
about 50%
t4-preflop-structure-q2.explanation: Required equity = amount to call ÷ pot after the call = 5.5 ÷ 17.5 = 31.4%. 40% comes from mistaking the risk for the opponent’s full bet of 8: 8 ÷ (4 + 8 + 8) = 40%; 23% comes from adding the bet twice: 5.5 ÷ (12 + 2 × 5.5) = 23.9%; 50% reuses the pot-sized-bet α as if it were a calling threshold — three of the most common slips inside one question.

t4-preflop-structure-q3.question: Both are 3-bets, yet BB’s OOP 3-bet to 11 demands a higher fold rate (74% vs 67%) than BTN’s IP 3-bet to 8. The root cause is:
options: BB’s cards are worse, so it needs more folds
OOP has a lower postflop equity realization rate, so it must buy immediate fold pressure and a bigger pot with a larger sizing
BB has position and can slow-play
Sizing is purely a matter of personal style
t4-preflop-structure-q3.explanation: Realization rate is the independent variable behind sizing: acting last on every street, the out-of-position player struggles to reach showdown, so the same value hand needs more immediate compensation. Option one confuses hand strength with a structural requirement on the range; option three is backwards (BB is out of position); option four demotes a structural question to personal taste.

t4-preflop-structure-q4.question: After the 4-bet the SPR is about 1.9. The direct consequence is:
options: There is plenty of postflop room to keep playing slowly
The structure is close to jam-or-fold, so the 4-bet range must be polarised
Hands like AQo are exactly the right 4-bet candidates
SPR has nothing to do with how a 4-bet range is built
t4-preflop-structure-q4.explanation: At SPR ≈ 2 three streets compress into a single all-in, so marginal hands are too weak to call a jam and not strong enough to 4-bet — they leave, and only strong value plus bluffs remain, which is polarisation. Option one contradicts “almost no chips behind relative to the pot”; option three names the textbook dominated hand as the ideal 4-bet candidate; option four denies the causal chain of this section.

t4-preflop-structure-q5.question: From Example 3: CO must add 80 into a pot of 201.5 facing the jam (threshold about 40%), while KK holds roughly 47% against {QQ+, AK} once its own blockers are removed. The correct conclusion is:
options: KK never reaches the break-even jam point, so it should fold
KK clears the 40% threshold and should call; AQo and JJ do not, which shows the 4-bet value branch must itself survive a re-jam
40% is an MDF, so KK may call with 40% frequency
As long as the opponent’s 4-bet range contains bluffs, any two cards can call a jam
t4-preflop-structure-q5.explanation: Threshold = 80 ÷ 201.5 = 39.7%. KK’s ~47% clears it, so call; AQo’s ~30% and JJ’s ~37% do not, so fold — that boundary is exactly the test for “a hand may enter the 4-bet value branch only if it survives a re-jam”. Option one conflates “not good enough to jam” with “not good enough to call”, which are different thresholds; option three turns an equity threshold into a frequency quota; option four treats “bluffs exist” as a licence to call, ignoring that the bluff branch’s combo count is usually far smaller than the value branch’s and cannot lift the threshold.

t4-structure-economics-q1.question: 50/100 with a 1bb big-blind ante (pot 2.5bb); BTN opens to 2.25bb. The break-even fold frequency α for this steal is about:
t4-structure-economics-q1.explanation: α = b ÷ (P + b) = 2.25 ÷ 4.75 = 47.4%. The 60.0% figure is the same sizing with no ante (P = 1.5), which is exactly the comparison made above; 40.0% is the no-ante MDF, mixing up two different quantities; 33.3% comes from betting 50 into a pot of 100, a different ratio than this one.

t4-structure-economics-q2.question: Which statement about a 1bb big-blind ante and the big blind defense is correct:
options: The amount still to put in falls from 1.25bb to 0.25bb, required equity drops from 25.0% to 5.0%, so the actual defense range should widen
The ante makes defending harder for the big blind, so the range should tighten
The ante only changes the size of the pot, not any defense frequency
Required equity rises from 5.0% to 25.0%, so only stronger hands may call
t4-structure-economics-q2.explanation: The ante is already in the pot, so the amount still needed falls while the pot after calling stays the same (5.0bb either way): 0.25 ÷ 5.0 = 5.0%, and a better price justifies a wider defense. Option 2 reads a higher MDF as "harder to defend", which is the opposite direction; option 3 denies that P is an argument of α and MDF, contradicting the whole chapter; option 4 swaps the two numbers and calls an improvement a worsening.

t4-structure-economics-q3.question: Gross winrate 8bb/100 is compressed to a net 3bb/100 by rake, with σ and the confidence multiplier unchanged. The hands needed to prove that edge become about:
options: about 1/7 of the original
about 7.1 times the original
essentially unchanged, you just win less per hundred
about 2.7 times the original
t4-structure-economics-q3.explanation: In n = (z·σ ÷ μ)² the μ sits in the denominator and is squared, so the multiplier is (8 ÷ 3)² ≈ 7.11. The 2.7 answer is 8/3, treating a squared relation as linear; the 1/7 answer inverts the ratio; "unchanged" forgets that μ is simultaneously the profit and the yardstick of significance - compress it and both proving the edge and surviving on it get harder at once.

t4-structure-economics-q4.question: A big-blind ante and a 1bb straddle both lift the pot from 1.5bb to 2.5bb. The key difference between them is:
options: A straddle is a bet while an ante is not, so only the straddle changes α
They are exactly equivalent, with no strategic difference
A straddle additionally buys one player the last preflop action, like paying 1bb for position; an ante does not change the order of action
Antes only exist in tournaments while straddles only exist in cash games
t4-structure-economics-q4.explanation: The dead-money effect is identical - α 47.4% and MDF 52.6% carry over between the two. The real difference is order of action: the straddler acts last preflop, so their own range can widen while the opener faces an extra opponent with position and must tighten somewhat. Option 1 treats the straddle as a bet branch, but it only enters P and never changes b; option 2 denies a difference that does change ranges; option 4 reverses how the two are actually distributed across formats.

t4-structure-economics-q5.question: At a heavy-rake micro stakes table taking about 5bb/100, which kind of action stops being profitable first?
options: Shoving KK into a 4-bet pot
Calling an all-in with AA from the big blind
Value betting a nut flush draw
Thin 3-bet bluffs and marginal calls, where the single-iteration edge is tiny
t4-structure-economics-q5.explanation: Rake takes a percentage of every pot, so the first casualties are actions that earn next to nothing per iteration and depend on enormous repetition - thin 3-bet bluffs and marginal calls are exactly that class. The other three share one property: the single-iteration win dwarfs the rake on that pot, whether it is thick value with an extreme hand or value betting a monster draw.
